newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Search for stricken sheep ship closing in.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Search for stricken sheep ship closing in.

text.p: The fate of almost 70,000 Australian sheep on a stricken vessel which caught fire bound for Jordan is expected to be known soon as a tug and a freighter search waters east of the Seychelles in the Indian Ocean.

"It's just around now that the vessels are getting to it and we'll have a more accurate fix then, if of course its still above the surface," Robin Poke, spokesman for the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), told Reuters on Friday.
The vessel had not been sighted yet, he said.
A disaster of the present type was very rare, given the number of live sheep exported from Australia each year, he said.
The 14,990 tonne Panama-flagged Uniceb was carrying an average-sized cargo of Australian sheep.
Shipments ranged from 35,000 to 120,000 live sheep, with average carrying capacity 73,000 sheep, a spokeswoman for the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp said.
"It's a fairly evocative instance when live animals are involved," Poke said.
The search for the Uniceb is being conducted by a tug, from Djibouti, on the Gulf of Aden, and the Cormo Express, a converted car carrier from Karachi, Pakistan.
The Uniceb caught fire Monday bound for the Jordanian port of Aqaba from Fremantle, Western Australia, and was abandoned by crew.
One crew member was killed and 54 rescued.
The ship left Fremantle on August 23 on an expected 16-day journey.

Last sighting of the Uniceb, hit by a fire which started in its engine room and spread to crew accomodation, was 400 km east of the Seychelles. The fate of the sheep has not been known since Monday and would not be known until the vessel was reached, AMLC spokesmen said on Friday.
The Cormo Express, now searching for the Uniceb, had unloaded sheep in Karachi and was headed back to Fremantle when diverted, they said.
Faced with a barrage of criticism from animal welfare groups and unions, the AMLC was at pains to defend its safety record.
Lloyd Beeby, head of the authority's sheepmeat and livestock marketing division, stressed that livestock vessels must conform with stringent requirements laid down by AMSA.
Ships in recent years had been refused the right to export live animals from Australia because they had not met AMSA requirements, he said.
Live sheep aboard ship were transported in pens, whose size and shape varied according to the configuration of the ship, Beeby said.
Some pens could be five metres by three metres, others two metres by two metres, others 10 metres by three metres, he said.
The number of sheep per pen would vary according to the size of sheep and the amount of wool they carried. There could be 20-30 sheep up to more than 100 sheep per pen, he said.
Ships had modern pump watering, with every new ship incorporating new techniques, he said.

In some ships, feeding was performed automatically, while in others feed was dropped from the roof through chutes to many points on each deck. Feed was then transported by wheelbarrows and hand-delivered by the crew, he said.
Each pen had multiple feed and water troughs and were cleaned by crews after feeding, he said.
Regulations set minimum heights of pens.
The walls of pens would not necessarily run from floor to ceiling, he said.
Beeby could not comment on systems used on the Uniceb.

Australia exported 5.54 million live sheep in 1995/96, most for slaughter. Of these, 1.57 million went to the largest market, Jordan, 1.41 million to the United Arab Emirates, 1.09 million to Kuwait, with smaller numbers going to Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Lebanon, Israel, Egypt, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Croatia. Value of exports was A$208 million.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
